title: Chapter 135 — The Chase.—Third Day
paragraphs: The third morning dawned fair and fresh, and once again the lone night-watchman at the fore-masthead was relieved by crowds of daytime lookouts, who dotted every mast and nearly every spar.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab; but the whale was not yet in sight.

"In his infallible wake, though; just follow that wake, that's all. Helm there; steady, as you go and have been going. What a lovely day again! If it were a new-made world, made for a summer-house for the angels, and this morning the first of its throwing open to them, a fairer day could not dawn upon that world. Here's food for thought, if Ahab had time to think; but Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels; and that is tingling enough for mortal man! To think is audacity. God alone has that right and privilege. Thinking is, or ought to be, a coolness and a calmness; and our poor hearts throb, and our poor brains beat, too much for that. And yet I've sometimes thought my brain was very calm — frozen calm, this old skull cracks so, like a glass whose contents have turned to ice and shivered it. And still this hair is growing now; growing this moment, and heat must breed it; but no, it's like that sort of common grass that will grow anywhere, between the earthy clefts of Greenland ice or in Vesuvius lava. How the wild winds blow it; they whip it about me as the torn shreds of split sails lash the tossed ship they cling to. A vile wind that has no doubt blown before this through prison corridors and cells, and hospital wards, and aired them out, and now comes blowing here as innocent as fleeces. Away with it! — it's tainted. If I were the wind, I'd blow no more on such a wicked, miserable world. I'd crawl off somewhere to a cave, and slink there. And yet the wind is a noble and heroic thing! Who ever conquered it? In every fight it has the last and bitterest blow. Run tilting at it, and you only run through it. Ha! a coward wind that strikes stark-naked men, but will not stand to receive a single blow. Even Ahab is a braver thing — a nobler thing than that. If only the wind had a body now; but all the things that most exasperate and outrage mortal man, all these things are bodiless — but bodiless only as objects, not as agents. There's a most special, a most cunning, oh, a most malicious difference! And yet, I say again, and swear it now, that there's something all glorious and gracious in the wind. These warm Trade Winds, at least, that blow straight on in the clear heavens, in strong and steadfast, vigorous mildness, and do not veer from their mark, however the baser currents of the sea may turn and tack, and the mightiest Mississippis of the land rush and swerve about, uncertain where to go at last. And by the eternal Poles! these same Trades that blow my good ship on so directly — these Trades, or something like them — something as unchangeable, and just as strong, blow my keeled soul along! To it! Aloft there! What do you see?"
"Nothing, sir."

"Nothing! And noon at hand! The doubloon goes begging! Look at the sun! Aye, aye, it must be so. I've oversailed him. How? Did he get the start? Aye, he's chasing me now — not I chasing him; that's bad; I might have known it, too. Fool! The lines — the harpoons he's towing. Aye, aye, I ran past him last night. About! About! Come down, all of you, except the regular lookouts! Man the braces!"

Because of the way she had been steering, the wind had been somewhat on the Pequod's quarter; so now, pointed in the reverse direction, the braced ship sailed close to the wind as she churned up again the cream of her own white wake.

"Against the wind he now steers for the open jaw," murmured Starbuck to himself, as he coiled the newly hauled main-brace on the rail. "God keep us, but already my bones feel damp inside me, and they wet my flesh from within. I fear that I disobey my God in obeying him!"
"Stand by to sway me up!" cried Ahab, advancing to the hempen basket. "We should meet him soon."
"Aye, aye, sir," and at once Starbuck did Ahab's bidding, and once more Ahab swung on high.

A whole hour now passed, beaten out like gold into ages. Time itself now held long breaths in keen suspense. But at last, some three points off the weather bow, Ahab sighted the spout again, and instantly three shrieks went up from the three mastheads, as if tongues of fire had voiced them.

"Forehead to forehead I meet you, this third time, Moby Dick! On deck there! — brace sharper up; crowd her into the wind's eye. He's too far off to lower yet, Mr. Starbuck. The sails shake! Stand over that helmsman with a top-maul! So, so; he travels fast, and I must go down. But let me have one more good round look aloft here at the sea; there's time for that. An old, old sight, and yet somehow so young; aye, and not changed a wink since I first saw it, a boy, from the sand-hills of Nantucket! The same! — the same! — the same to Noah as to me. There's a soft shower to leeward. Such lovely leewardings! They must lead somewhere — to something other than common land, more palmy than the palms. Leeward! The white whale goes that way; look to windward, then; the better if the bitterer quarter. But good-bye, good-bye, old masthead! What's this? — green? Aye, tiny mosses in these warped cracks. No such green weather-stains on Ahab's head! There's the difference now between man's old age and matter's. But aye, old mast, we both grow old together; sound in our hulls, though, are we not, my ship? Aye, minus a leg, that's all. By heaven, this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way. I can't compare with it; and I've known some ships made of dead trees outlast the lives of men made of the most vital stuff of vital fathers. What's that he said? He should still go before me, my pilot, and yet be seen again? But where? Will I have eyes at the bottom of the sea, supposing I go down those endless stairs? And all night I've been sailing away from him, wherever he sank to. Aye, aye, like many more, you told dire truth about yourself, O Parsee; but, Ahab, there your shot fell short. Good-bye, masthead — keep a good eye on the whale while I'm gone. We'll talk tomorrow — no, tonight, when the white whale lies down there, tied by head and tail."
He gave the order, and, still looking all around him, was lowered steadily through the split blue air to the deck.

In due time the boats were lowered; but as Ahab, standing in the stern of his boat, hovered just at the point of descending, he waved to the mate — who held one of the tackle-ropes on deck — and told him to pause.
"Starbuck!"
"Sir?"
"For the third time my soul's ship sets out on this voyage, Starbuck."
"Aye, sir, you will have it so."
"Some ships sail from their ports and are missing ever afterward, Starbuck!"
"Truth, sir: saddest truth."
"Some men die at ebb tide; some at low water; some at the full of the flood; — and I feel now like a billow that's all one crested comb, Starbuck. I am old; — shake hands with me, man."
Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck's tears were the glue.
"Oh, my captain, my captain! — noble heart — don't go — don't go! — see, it's a brave man that weeps; how great, then, the agony of the pleading!"
"Lower away!" cried Ahab, tossing the mate's arm from him. "Stand by the crew!"
In an instant the boat was pulling round close under the stern.
"The sharks! The sharks!" cried a voice from the low cabin window there. "O master, my master, come back!"
But Ahab heard nothing, for just then his own voice was raised high; and the boat sprang on.

Yet the voice spoke true; for he had scarcely pushed off from the ship when numbers of sharks, seemingly rising out of the dark waters beneath the hull, snapped maliciously at the oar blades every time they dipped into the water, and in this way kept the boat company with their bites. It is a thing that not uncommonly happens to whaleboats in those swarming seas, the sharks at times apparently following them with the same foresight with which vultures hover over the banners of marching regiments in the east. But these were the first sharks the Pequod had observed since the White Whale was first sighted; and whether it was that Ahab's crew were all such tiger-yellow barbarians, and their flesh therefore more musky to the sharks' senses — a thing sometimes well known to affect them — however it was, they seemed to follow that one boat without molesting the others.

"Heart of wrought steel!" murmured Starbuck, gazing over the side and following the receding boat with his eyes — "can you still ring boldly to that sight? — lowering your keel among ravening sharks, and followed by them, open-mouthed, to the chase; and this the critical third day? — For when three days flow together in one continuous, intense pursuit, be sure the first is the morning, the second the noon, and the third the evening and the end of that thing — whatever that end may be. Oh, my God! what is this that shoots through me and leaves me so deadly calm, yet expectant — fixed at the top of a shudder! Future things swim before me, as in empty outlines and skeletons; all the past has somehow grown dim. Mary, girl! you fade in pale glories behind me; boy! I seem to see nothing of you but your eyes, grown wondrous blue. The strangest problems of life seem to be clearing; but clouds sweep between — Is my journey's end coming? My legs feel faint, like those of a man who has been on foot all day. Feel your heart — does it still beat? Stir yourself, Starbuck! — stave it off — move, move! Speak aloud! — Masthead there! Do you see my boy's hand on the hill? — Crazed; — aloft there! — keep your keenest eye on the boats — mark the whale well! — Ho! again! — drive off that hawk! See! he pecks — he tears the vane" — pointing to the red flag flying at the main-truck, the cap at the very top of the mainmast — "Ha! he soars away with it! — Where's the old man now? Do you see that sight, oh Ahab! — shudder, shudder!"

The boats had not gone very far when, by a signal from the mastheads — an arm pointed downward — Ahab knew that the whale had sounded; but meaning to be near him at his next rising, he held on his way a little to one side of the vessel, the spellbound crew keeping the deepest silence as the head-on waves hammered and hammered against the opposing bow.
"Drive, drive in your nails, oh you waves! Drive them in to their very heads! You only strike a thing without a lid; and no coffin and no hearse can be mine — and only hemp can kill me! Ha! ha!"

Suddenly the waters around them slowly swelled in broad circles; then quickly heaved up, as if sliding sideways off a submerged iceberg swiftly rising to the surface. A low rumbling sound was heard, a hum from under the earth; and then all held their breath, as, draggled with trailing ropes and harpoons and lances, a vast form shot lengthwise, but slantwise, from the sea. Shrouded in a thin, drooping veil of mist, it hovered for a moment in the rainbowed air, and then fell swamping back into the deep. Crushed thirty feet upward, the waters flashed for an instant like heaps of fountains, then sank brokenly in a shower of flakes, leaving the circling surface creamed like new milk round the marble trunk of the whale.

"Give way!" cried Ahab to the oarsmen, and the boats darted forward to the attack; but, maddened by yesterday's fresh irons corroding in him, Moby Dick seemed possessed by all the angels that fell from heaven at once. The wide tiers of welded tendons spreading over his broad white forehead beneath the transparent skin looked knitted together, as he came on head first, churning his tail among the boats, and once more flailed them apart, spilling the irons and lances out of the two mates' boats and smashing in one side of the upper part of their bows, but leaving Ahab's almost without a scar.

While Daggoo and Queequeg were stopping up the strained planks, and as the whale, swimming out from them, turned and showed one entire flank as he shot past them again, at that moment a quick cry went up. Lashed round and round to the fish's back, pinned in the turns upon turns in which the whale had wound the coils of the lines around himself during the past night, the half-torn body of the Parsee was seen, his black garments frayed to shreds, his bulging eyes turned full upon old Ahab.
The harpoon dropped from his hand.

"Fooled, fooled!" — drawing in a long, lean breath — "Aye, Parsee! I see you again. — Aye, and you go before; and this — this, then — is the hearse that you promised. But I hold you to the last letter of your word. Where is the second hearse? Away, mates, to the ship! Those boats are useless now; repair them if you can in time, and return to me; if not, Ahab is enough to die — Down, men! The first thing that so much as offers to jump from this boat I stand in, that thing I harpoon. You are not other men, but my arms and my legs; so obey me. — Where's the whale? Gone down again?"

But he looked too near the boat; for, as if bent on escaping with the corpse he carried, and as if the particular place of the last encounter had been only a stage in his voyage to leeward, Moby Dick was now again swimming steadily forward, and had almost passed the ship — which so far had been sailing in the opposite direction to him, though for the present her headway had been stopped. He seemed to be swimming at his utmost speed, and now intent only on pursuing his own straight path in the sea.
"Oh! Ahab," cried Starbuck, "it is not too late, even now, the third day, to stop. See! Moby Dick does not seek you. It is you, you, that madly seek him!"

Setting sail to the rising wind, the lonely boat was driven swiftly to leeward by both oars and canvas. And at last, as Ahab was sliding past the vessel, so near that he could plainly make out Starbuck's face as he leaned over the rail, he hailed him to turn the vessel about and follow him, not too swiftly, at a judicious interval. Glancing upward, he saw Tashtego, Queequeg, and Daggoo eagerly climbing to the three mastheads, while the oarsmen were rocking in the two staved boats, which had just been hoisted to the side, busily at work repairing them. One after another, through the portholes, as he sped by, he also caught flying glimpses of Stubb and Flask busying themselves on deck among bundles of new irons and lances. As he saw all this, as he heard the hammers in the broken boats, far different hammers seemed to be driving a nail into his heart. But he rallied. And now, noticing that the vane or flag was gone from the main-masthead, he shouted to Tashtego, who had just reached that perch, to come down again for another flag, and a hammer and nails, and so nail it to the mast.

Whether he was worn out by the three days' running chase and by the drag of the knotted tangle he carried, or whether it was some hidden deceitfulness and malice in him — whichever was true, the White Whale's speed now began, as it seemed from the boat so rapidly nearing him once more, to slacken; though indeed the whale's last start had not been so long a one as before. And still, as Ahab glided over the waves, the pitiless sharks went with him, and stuck so doggedly to the boat, and bit so continually at the plying oars, that the blades became jagged and crunched, and left small splinters in the sea at almost every dip.
"Pay them no heed! Those teeth only give your oars new rowlocks. Pull on! The shark's jaw is a better rest than the yielding water."
"But at every bite, sir, the thin blades grow smaller and smaller!"

"They will last long enough! Pull on! — But who can tell," he muttered, "whether these sharks swim to feast on the whale or on Ahab? — But pull on! Aye, all alive now — we're nearing him. The helm! Take the helm! Let me pass" — and with that, two of the oarsmen helped him forward to the bow of the still-flying boat.

At length, as the boat was cast to one side and ran along level with the White Whale's flank, he seemed strangely unaware of its approach — as the whale sometimes will be — and Ahab was right inside the smoky mountain of mist which, thrown off from the whale's spout, curled around his great Monadnock hump. He was that close to him when, with his body arched back and both arms raised high lengthwise to the poise, he darted his fierce iron, and his far fiercer curse, into the hated whale. As both steel and curse sank in to the socket, as if sucked into a morass, Moby Dick writhed sideways, rolled his near flank convulsively against the bow, and, without staving a hole in it, tipped the boat over so suddenly that, if it had not been for the raised part of the gunwale he then clung to, Ahab would once more have been thrown into the sea. As it was, three of the oarsmen — who had not known beforehand the exact instant of the dart, and were therefore unprepared for its effects — were flung out; but they fell in such a way that in an instant two of them clutched the gunwale again and, rising to its level on a combing wave, hurled themselves bodily back inboard; the third man dropped helplessly astern, but was still afloat and swimming.

Almost at the same moment, with a mighty act of will and a swiftness that came instantly, all at once, the White Whale darted through the weltering sea. But when Ahab called to the steersman to take new turns with the line and hold it so, and ordered the crew to turn round on their seats and tow the boat up to the mark, the moment the treacherous line felt that double strain and tug, it snapped in the empty air!
"What breaks in me? Some sinew cracks! — it's whole again; oars! oars! Burst in upon him!"

Hearing the tremendous rush of the sea-crashing boat, the whale wheeled round to present his blank forehead at bay; but in that turn, catching sight of the black hull of the ship drawing near, seemingly seeing in it the source of all his persecutions, taking it — it may be — for a larger and nobler foe, he suddenly bore down on its advancing prow, clashing his jaws amid fiery showers of foam.
Ahab staggered; his hand struck his forehead. "I'm growing blind; hands! stretch out before me so that I may still grope my way. Is it night?"
"The whale! The ship!" cried the cringing oarsmen.

"Oars! oars! Slope downward to your depths, O sea, so that before it is forever too late, Ahab may slide this last, last time upon his mark! I see: the ship! the ship! Dash on, my men! Will you not save my ship?"

But as the oarsmen violently forced their boat through the sledgehammering seas, the bow-ends of two planks that the whale had already struck burst through, and almost in an instant the temporarily disabled boat lay nearly level with the waves, its half-wading, splashing crew trying hard to stop the gap and bail out the pouring water.

Meanwhile, for that one instant of watching, Tashtego's masthead hammer stayed suspended in his hand; and the red flag, half wrapping him like a plaid, then streamed straight out from him, like his own forward-flowing heart; while Starbuck and Stubb, standing on the bowsprit below, caught sight of the oncoming monster just as soon as he did.

"The whale, the whale! Up helm, up helm! Oh, all you sweet powers of air, hold me close now! Let not Starbuck die, if die he must, in a woman's fainting fit. Up helm, I say — you fools, the jaw! the jaw! Is this the end of all my bursting prayers? all my lifelong fidelities? Oh, Ahab, Ahab, behold your work. Steady! helmsman, steady. No, no! Up helm again! He turns to meet us! Oh, his unappeasable brow drives on toward one whose duty tells him he cannot depart. My God, stand by me now!"

"Don't stand by me, but stand under me, whoever you are that will now help Stubb; for Stubb, too, sticks here. I grin at you, you grinning whale! Who ever helped Stubb, or kept Stubb awake, but Stubb's own unwinking eye? And now poor Stubb goes to bed on a mattress that is all too soft; I wish it were stuffed with brushwood! I grin at you, you grinning whale! Look here, sun, moon, and stars! I call you assassins of as good a fellow as ever spouted up his ghost. For all that, I would still clink glasses with you, if you would only hand the cup! Oh, oh! oh, oh! you grinning whale, but there'll be plenty of gulping soon! Why don't you fly, O Ahab! For me, off with shoes and jacket for it; let Stubb die in his drawers! A most moldy and oversalted death, though — cherries! cherries! cherries! Oh, Flask, for one red cherry before we die!"
"Cherries? I only wish that we were where they grow. Oh, Stubb, I hope my poor mother has drawn my part-pay before now; if not, few coppers will come to her now, for the voyage is up."

From the ship's bows nearly all the seamen now hung idle, hammers, bits of plank, lances, and harpoons still mechanically held in their hands, just as they had rushed from their various jobs; all their spellbound eyes were fixed on the whale, which, strangely swinging his predestinating head from side to side, sent a broad band of spreading, semicircular foam before him as he rushed. Retribution, swift vengeance, eternal malice were in his whole aspect, and in spite of all that mortal man could do, the solid white buttress of his forehead struck the ship's starboard bow, till men and timbers reeled. Some fell flat on their faces. Like dislodged trucks, the heads of the harpooners aloft shook on their bull-like necks. Through the breach they heard the waters pour, like mountain torrents down a flume.
"The ship! The hearse! — the second hearse!" cried Ahab from the boat. "Its wood could only be American!"

Diving beneath the settling ship, the whale ran quivering along its keel; but, turning under water, he shot swiftly to the surface again, far off the other bow, but within a few yards of Ahab's boat, where for a time he lay still.

"I turn my body from the sun. What ho, Tashtego! Let me hear your hammer. Oh! you three unsurrendered spires of mine; you uncracked keel; and only god-bullied hull; you firm deck, and haughty helm, and Pole-pointed prow — death-glorious ship! must you then perish, and without me? Am I cut off from the last fond pride of the meanest shipwrecked captains? Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief. Ho, ho! from all your farthest bounds, pour in now, you bold billows of my whole bygone life, and top this one piled comber of my death! Toward you I roll, you all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with you; from hell's heart I stab at you; for hate's sake I spit my last breath at you. Sink all coffins and all hearses to one common pool! and since neither can be mine, let me then be towed to pieces, while still chasing you, though tied to you, you damned whale! Thus, I give up the spear!"

The harpoon was thrown; the wounded whale shot forward; the line ran through the grooves with igniting speed — and fouled. Ahab bent down to clear it; he did clear it; but the flying loop caught him around the neck, and as silently as Turkish mutes strangle their victim with the bowstring, he was jerked out of the boat before the crew knew he was gone. The next instant the heavy eye-splice at the very end of the rope flew out of the completely empty tub, knocked down an oarsman, and, hitting the sea, vanished into its depths.

For an instant the entranced boat's crew stood still; then turned. "The ship? Great God, where is the ship?" Soon, through dim, bewildering mediums, they saw her sidelong fading phantom, as in the gaseous Fata Morgana mirage, only the uppermost masts out of the water; while, fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate to their once lofty perches, the pagan harpooners still kept their sinking lookouts on the sea. And now concentric circles seized the lone boat itself, and all its crew, and each floating oar, and every lance-pole, and, spinning animate and inanimate all round and round in one vortex, carried the smallest chip of the Pequod out of sight.

But as the last floods poured, mingling, over the sunken head of the Indian at the mainmast, leaving a few inches of the upright spar still visible, together with long streaming yards of the flag, which calmly rippled, with ironic coincidence, over the destroying billows they almost touched — at that instant a red arm and a hammer hovered, raised backward in the open air, in the act of nailing the flag faster and yet faster to the sinking spar. A sky-hawk that had tauntingly followed the main-truck downward from its natural home among the stars, pecking at the flag and harassing Tashtego there, now happened to put its broad fluttering wing between the hammer and the wood; and at the same moment, feeling that ethereal thrill, the submerged savage below, in his death-gasp, kept his hammer frozen there; and so the bird of heaven, with archangelic shrieks, his imperial beak thrust upward, and his whole captive form folded in the flag of Ahab, went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell until she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her and helmeted herself with it.

Now little birds flew screaming over the gulf, which still gaped open; a sullen white surf beat against its steep sides; then everything collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it had rolled five thousand years ago.
